title: Padre Pio (1887–1968)
hook: a Capuchin friar known for long confessions and the stigmata

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict XV, who called the Great War a useless slaughter and offered a plan for peace. Your line was useless slaughter. Did you ask what it would take to stop? Today, a friar in a small town, and a very long line. Day nine hundred five.

Two hands in brown fingerless gloves, resting on the edge of a confessional. In San Giovanni Rotondo, a town on a mountainside in southern Italy, people gather outside a friary church before dawn to kneel in front of those hands. Farmers, visitors from far away, people who haven't been to church in years. They're not there for a show. They want a few minutes with a bearded Capuchin friar in a brown habit. The gloves cover something he would rather not put on display. His name is Padre Pio.
screen: `TWO GLOVED HANDS.` → `A CROWD BEFORE DAWN.` → `A FRIAR IN A BROWN HABIT.`

segments.voice: Four sides of the man. First, the confessional. Padre Pio spent long hours, day after day, hearing confessions. People said he could be gentle and also blunt; tradition says he sometimes sent a person away to come back more honest. Second, the wounds. He carried marks on his hands, feet and side, like the wounds of Christ, the stigmata. That's why the gloves. Catholics hear Saint Paul in the letter to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body." Doctors examined him. Some were convinced, some skeptical. Third, the obedience. Church authorities investigated him more than once, and for a time they restricted his ministry, keeping him from saying Mass in public and from hearing confessions. He obeyed, and waited. The restrictions were later eased. When the Church canonized him, it honored his holiness of life; Catholics remain free to judge the wounds for themselves. Fourth, the work and the advice. He built a hospital in the town, the Home for the Relief of Suffering, and encouraged people to form prayer groups. And there is a line attributed to him that people still repeat, simple enough to fit on a fridge magnet: pray, hope, and don't worry. Three short verbs. For a friar who spent his days hearing the worst of people's lives, it is a surprisingly light thing to say.
screen: `HOURS IN THE CONFESSIONAL.` · `THE MARKS OF CHRIST.` · `INVESTIGATED, AND OBEDIENT.` · `PRAY, HOPE, DON'T WORRY.` · then, large: `I BEAR THE MARKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go to confession, or take one step toward it. Settle, and breathe. Picture that crowd outside his church before dawn, and yourself somewhere in it. When your turn came, what would you want to set down? Let one honest sentence form. If you're Catholic, you might find your parish's confession times and choose a day this week. If you're not, you might ask who that sentence is owed to, and what you could say to them. Either way, end with the friar's three words: pray, hope, don't worry. The bell holds the time.
Padre Pio. A Capuchin friar in southern Italy, known for long hours of confession and the wounds of the stigmata.
Your line: pray, hope, don't worry. Today, when one worry starts to loop, say those three words to yourself and then do one useful thing about it. Day nine hundred five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Padre Pio's memorial in September; pilgrims visit San Giovanni Rotondo, Padre Pio prayer groups meet in parishes, and Catholics go to confession, often on Saturdays or before great feasts.

options: keep going anyway: the people need you.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint famous for miracles.
what it means: a confessor who spent long hours with sinners, carried wounds like Christ's, and obeyed when restricted.
what a scholar hears: canonization honored his holiness of life; it doesn't require Catholics to hold a view on the stigmata.
